title: AWS CLF-C02 vs SAA-C03: Which to Take First?
subtitle: Cloud Practitioner first, or straight to Solutions Architect?

pros: No prerequisites and built for beginners: you can pass it without ever having opened the AWS console.
Realistic prep of 40-60 hours — roughly 4-6 weeks part-time, versus 3-4 months for the SAA.
The cheapest exam in the AWS lineup ($100): a low-cost way to confirm you actually enjoy cloud work.
Covers the cross-cutting vocabulary (Regions, IAM, the shared responsibility model, billing) that every role needs, technical or not.
cons: Weak résumé signal on its own for a technical role: a Cloud Engineer recruiter expects the SAA, not the CLF.
Zero architectural depth — no VPC design, no sizing, no failure scenarios.
Often seen as a 'warm-up cert': rarely enough on its own to land a first cloud job.
certs.bestFor: You are completely new to cloud, or you work in a non-technical role (sales, project management, finance) at a cloud-adjacent company.

pros: The reference cloud cert on the job market: it is the one recruiters name in Cloud Engineer / Architect job postings.
Senior median salary of €65k in France versus €52k for a profile that stopped at the CLF (indicative estimates).
Tests real design: VPCs, sizing, multi-AZ high availability, service selection, cost optimization.
Leads straight into the rest of the Associate/Pro track (Developer, SysOps, then Solutions Architect Professional).
cons: A technical exam: hard to target directly if you have never administered infrastructure or used AWS.
Realistic prep of 120-150 hours — plan for 3-4 months at 8-10 hours per week.
$150 per attempt, and a fail is expensive in time: better to show up ready.
certs.bestFor: You already have a tech background (developer, sysadmin, ops, tier-2/3 support) and want the credential that actually unlocks cloud jobs.

verdicts.profile: You are a total beginner — never touched cloud or infrastructure.
verdicts.why: Start with the CLF-C02: it gives you AWS vocabulary and the mental model in 4-6 weeks without drowning you. You will then tackle the SAA on solid footing instead of struggling through it.

verdicts.profile: You are already a developer, sysadmin or ops engineer and want a cloud role.
verdicts.why: Skip the CLF: your background already covers 80% of it. Going straight for the SAA saves you $100 and 6 weeks, and it is the one that appears in job postings.

verdicts.profile: You work in a non-technical role (sales, project management, recruiting, finance) at a cloud company.
verdicts.why: The CLF-C02 is made for you: it gives you the shared language to talk credibly about cloud with technical teams, without demanding architecture design you will never use.

verdicts.profile: You want the strongest résumé signal to land a Cloud Engineer or Architect job.
verdicts.why: The SAA-C03 is the one recruiters recognize and require. The CLF on its own often goes unnoticed in a stack of applications for a technical role.

verdicts.profile: Tight budget and timeline — you want a quick result.
verdicts.why: The CLF is faster (40-60 hours) and cheaper ($100). It is a real first milestone on your résumé, as long as you treat it as a step toward the SAA, not a destination.

verdicts.profile: You plan to take both anyway.
verdicts.why: Take the CLF-C02 first as a 4-6 week warm-up: it locks in the fundamentals the SAA assumes. You then move on to the SAA with less review time needed.

tldr: CLF-C02 = AWS vocabulary, beginner-friendly, but a weak résumé signal on its own. SAA-C03 = the real cert that opens cloud jobs and pushes salary up. Complete beginner → start with the CLF. Solid tech background already → skip it and go straight for the SAA.
